pos: n. (Raymond Lull, c. 1232–1316, Majorcan layman, philosopher and missionary to the Muslims, author of the Ars Magna and the first Western advocate of learning Arabic to preach to Arabs)
etymology: Catalan Ramon Llull; Latinized Raimundus Lullus. Also written Lully.
biblical_def: Raymond Lull was a courtier of Majorca who, converted in his thirties, gave the rest of a long life to one purpose: the conversion of the Muslim world by argument rather than by crusade. He learned Arabic from a slave he bought for the purpose, spent nine years in study, and then petitioned popes, kings and councils to found chairs of Arabic and Hebrew so that missionaries could reason with Muslims in their own tongue — a request the Council of Vienne finally granted in 1311. He crossed to North Africa three times to dispute publicly in Tunis and Bugia, was imprisoned and expelled, and by the oldest tradition was stoned at Bugia in extreme old age. His method is the apostle's: Paul “reasoned with them out of the scriptures” (Act 17:2), and Apollos “mightily convinced the Jews, and that publickly, shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ” (Act 18:28). 2Co 5:11 gives the motive — “Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men.” His Ars Magna, a system of combinatory figures meant to generate all truth, is a curiosity; his insistence that the gospel travels by persuasion and not by the sword was three centuries ahead of Christendom.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to persuade as to influence by argument, advice, intreaty or expostulation; to draw or incline the will to a determination by presenting motives to the mind.
webster_full: PERSUA'DE, v.t. To influence by argument, advice, intreaty or expostulation; to draw or incline the will to a determination by presenting motives to the mind.
2. To convince by argument, or reasons offered.
CONVINCE, v.t. To persuade or satisfy the mind by evidence.
scriptures: Act 17:2
And Paul, as his manner was, went in unto them, and three sabbath days reasoned with them out of the scriptures,
For he mightily convinced the Jews, and that publickly, shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ.
Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men; but we are made manifest unto God; and I trust also are made manifest in your consciences.
Jud 1:3

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
corruption_summary: Lull asked Christendom to argue where it preferred to fight, and Christendom gave him a chair of Arabic and went on crusading.
corruption_paragraphs: The crusading assumption — that unbelief is to be answered with armies — is the standing corruption Lull opposed, and it is a denial of the nature of faith. A man cannot be conquered into believing, and the apostolic method is reasoning, persuading and shewing from the Scriptures. Lull did not oppose the crusade consistently and at times urged a military wing to his missionary programme, which is the mark of his century on him; the better instinct is the one that sent him to dispute in Tunis alone. Jud 1:3 commands that we “earnestly contend for the faith,” and the contending is argument, not arms.

The opposite corruption is the modern one, and it is now the greater danger: the refusal to contend at all, on the ground that argument is impolite and that other religions are parallel paths. Lull would have thought that a stranger error than the crusade. He went where he could be stoned because he believed the Muslim was lost and the gospel true, and 2Co 5:11 says plainly what moved him. The recovery is Lull's own combination, stripped of his century's sword: learn the language, master the objections, go in person, and persuade.

“shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ” (Act 18:28) — public disputation.
“we persuade men” (2Co 5:11) — the motive that took him to Tunis.

pos: n. (Meister Eckhart, c. 1260–c. 1328, German Dominican preacher and speculative mystic, twenty-eight of whose propositions were condemned by Pope John XXII in 1329)
etymology: German Meister, master, his academic title; Eckhart from ecke, edge, and hart, hard. Eckhart von Hochheim.
biblical_def: Meister Eckhart was a Dominican provincial and a Paris master whose German sermons are among the most powerful ever preached in that language. His theme is the ground of the soul, a point at its centre where, he says, God and the soul meet without distinction; he speaks of an uncreated spark in man, of the birth of the Word in the soul, and of a detachment so complete that the soul wills nothing, not even God. Much of this is a straining after real things — union with Christ, the indwelling Spirit, self-denial — and his defenders argue that his daring language was pastoral paradox. But the propositions as they stand erase the line Scripture will not let be erased, between the Creator and the creature He made. Isa 42:8 is the boundary: “I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another.” Act 17:28 grants the nearness — “For in him we live, and move, and have our being” — without any confusion of beings. Joh 1:12 gives the only sonship on offer: to those who received Him “gave he power to become the sons of God,” a becoming by adoption and grace, not an uncreated identity already there.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pantheism as the doctrine that the universe is God, or that all things are God; and mysticism as obscurity of doctrine.
webster_full: PAN'THEISM, n. The doctrine that the universe is God, or the system of theology in which it is maintained that the universe is the supreme God.
PAN'THEIST, n. One that believes the universe to be God.
MYS'TICISM, n. Obscurity of doctrine. 2. The doctrine of the Mystics, who profess a pure, sublime and perfect devotion.
scriptures: Isa 42:8
I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images.
For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.
Rom 1:25
Who changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. Amen.
Joh 1:12
But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:
corruption_summary: Eckhart is the father of every spirituality that locates the divine in the depth of the self, and that is now the default religion of the educated West.
corruption_paragraphs: The uncreated ground of the soul is the seed of a vast modern harvest. Strip Eckhart of his Dominican vocabulary and what remains is the conviction that God is found by descending into the self, that the true self is divine, and that doctrine and ordinance are husks around that kernel. This is the common creed of therapeutic spirituality, of the perennialist account of all religions, and of a good deal of what is sold as contemplative Christianity. Rom 1:25 names the exchange it rests on: those “who changed the truth of God into a lie, and worshipped and served the creature more than the Creator.”

The recovery is the Creator-creature distinction held without apology, together with everything Scripture actually promises. The believer is united to Christ, indwelt by the Spirit, adopted as a son, conformed to the image of the Son and destined for glory — a nearness greater than Eckhart's and of a different kind, because it never stops being the nearness of two. Act 17:28 is as close as inspired language comes to his theme, and it is spoken of all men, pagans included, as a statement about dependence, not identity. God will not give His glory to another, and He does not need to, for He gives Himself.
roots_summary: Hebrew kabod (H3519), glory, weight; Greek ktisis (G2937), the creature, the thing created; teknon (G5043), a child.
roots_lines: Hebrew kabod (H3519) — glory, honour, weight; Isaiah 42:8.
Hebrew shem (H8034) — name; Isaiah 42:8.
Greek ktisis (G2937) — creation, the creature; Romans 1:25.
Greek teknon (G5043) — a child, by birth or adoption; John 1:12.
Greek exousia (G1849) — right, authority; John 1:12.

“For in him we live, and move, and have our being” (Act 17:28) — dependence, not identity.
“gave he power to become the sons of God” (Joh 1:12) — sonship given, not innate.

pos: n. (Johannes Tauler, c. 1300–1361, Dominican preacher of Strasbourg, Rhineland mystic and pastor through the Black Death, whose sermons Luther valued highly)
etymology: German Tauler, probably an occupational name; Johannes, the Latin form of John.
biblical_def: Johannes Tauler was Eckhart's pupil and is a far safer guide than his master. He preached in Strasbourg and Basel through the plague years and the papal interdict, when the sacraments were withheld from whole cities and he went on ministering to the dying. His sermons turn the speculative themes of the Rhineland school toward the ordinary Christian: self-knowledge, the mortifying of self-will, resignation to God's providence, the comfort of the humble. Luther republished the German Theology associated with his circle and said he had learned more from Tauler than from all the scholastics, and the reason is plain: Tauler keeps saying that man has nothing of his own to bring. Joh 15:5 is nearly his refrain — “without me ye can do nothing.” Mat 11:28 is his invitation, and Rom 8:16 his doctrine of assurance, that “The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God.” What is lacking is the forensic centre: Tauler leads the soul to resignation and detachment where Paul leads it to justification, so the comfort he offers rests on the soul's state rather than on Christ's finished work.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines resignation as submission; quiet submission to the will of Providence; and devotion as a yielding of the heart and affections to God.
webster_full: RESIGNA'TION, n. The act of resigning or quitting; as the resignation of a office.
2. Submission; quiet submission to the will of Providence; as resignation to the divine will.
DEVO'TION, n. The state of being dedicated, consecrated, or solemnly set apart for a particular purpose.
scriptures: Joh 15:5
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth.
Rom 8:16
The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God:
corruption_summary: Tauler brings the soul to resignation where Paul brings it to justification, and a comfort built on the soul's state will not hold in the dark.
corruption_paragraphs: The weakness of even the best medieval mysticism is where it locates peace. Tauler tells the troubled Christian to sink deeper, to abandon self-will, to rest in the ground of the soul; Paul tells him that “being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.” The difference is not emphasis but foundation. A peace that depends on having reached a sufficient detachment fails exactly when the soul is least able to detach, which is why Luther, who loved Tauler, had to go past him to Romans. Rom 8:16 is the right ground and it is the Spirit's witness to a finished work, not the soul's report on its own progress.

What should be kept is substantial, and the Reformed tradition has always known it. Tauler's insistence that the creature has nothing of its own is the very truth the nominalist schools had lost, and it prepared the Reformation more than many a sharper polemic. “without me ye can do nothing” (Joh 15:5) is monergism in six words. Read him for that, and for a pastor who stayed in a plague city; read Romans for the ground of standing.

roots_lines: Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, to remain; John 15:5.
Greek anapauo (G373) — to give rest, to refresh; Matthew 11:28.
Greek summartureo (G4828) — to bear witness together with; Romans 8:16.
Hebrew raphah (H7503) — to be still, to let go; Psalm 46:10.
Greek phortizo (G5412) — to be laden; Matthew 11:28.

“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden” (Mat 11:28) — the invitation he pressed.
“The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit” (Rom 8:16) — the ground of assurance.

pos: n. (Henry Suso, c. 1295–1366, Dominican of Constance, Rhineland mystic and author of the Little Book of Eternal Wisdom, famous for severe self-mortification which he later renounced)
biblical_def: Henry Suso was Eckhart's pupil and defended his master after the condemnation, but his own writing is devotional rather than speculative and was among the most widely read in late medieval Europe. The Little Book of Eternal Wisdom is a dialogue between the soul and Christ as Wisdom, built around the Passion, and its meditations on Isa 53:3 — “a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief” — are genuinely affecting. His Life describes sixteen years of extreme austerities: a hair shirt, an undergarment set with nails, a spiked cross bound to his back, sleep denied and food reduced, all undertaken to subdue the flesh. He eventually abandoned them on what he said was divine instruction and spent his later years as a gentle director of souls. Scripture supplies both the warrant he thought he had and the correction. Rom 8:13 commands that we “through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body,” and 1Co 9:27 that Paul kept under his body; but the mortifying is of deeds by the Spirit, not of flesh by iron, and Gal 2:20 locates the death where it was actually accomplished: “I am crucified with Christ.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mortification, in a theological sense, as the subduing of the passions and appetites by penance, abstinence, or painful severities inflicted on the body.
webster_full: MORTIFICA'TION, n. The act of subduing the passions and appetites by penance, abstinence, or painful severities inflicted on the body.
MOR'TIFY, v.t. To destroy the strength, vigor or activity of; to subdue; as, to mortify the appetites.
2. To subdue inordinate passions; to bring into subjection.
scriptures: Rom 8:13
For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live.
But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.
Gal 2:20

I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.
Isa 53:3
He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
corruption_summary: Suso tried for sixteen years to kill sin with iron and gave it up, which is the most useful thing he ever did.
corruption_paragraphs: Medieval mortification confused the flesh of Scripture with the body. Paul's sarx is the whole fallen nature, mind and will included, and it is not reached by a hair shirt; a man can wear nails and remain proud, and the austerity itself can feed the pride. Rom 8:13 names both the object and the agent: the deeds of the body are mortified “through the Spirit,” which makes sanctification a work of grace and not a feat of endurance. Suso's own abandonment of his instruments is the honest verdict of the experiment, and his later gentleness is worth more than his earlier iron.

The nearer corruption is the Protestant version that keeps the logic without the hardware — the believer who suspects that a harsher discipline, a stricter rule or a more punishing schedule will finally break a besetting sin. It will not. Gal 2:20 says the decisive death has happened: “I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me.” Real mortification follows from that union, is wrought by the Spirit through the ordinary means, and is fed by the sight of the man of sorrows rather than by imitation of His wounds.
roots_summary: Greek thanatoo (G2289), to put to death; hupopiazo (G5299), to keep under, to buffet; sustauroo (G4957), to crucify with.
roots_lines: Greek thanatoo (G2289) — to put to death, to mortify; Romans 8:13.
Greek hupopiazo (G5299) — to beat black and blue, to keep under; 1 Corinthians 9:27.
Greek adokimos (G96) — rejected, a castaway; 1 Corinthians 9:27.
Greek sustauroo (G4957) — to crucify together with; Galatians 2:20.
Hebrew makob (H4341) — pain, sorrow; Isaiah 53:3.

“I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection” (1Co 9:27) — the text he pressed too far.
“I am crucified with Christ” (Gal 2:20) — where the death was accomplished.

pos: n. (Gerard Groote, 1340–1384, preacher of Deventer and founder of the Brethren of the Common Life, from whom the Devotio Moderna and its schools sprang)
etymology: Dutch Geert Groote, Latinized Gerardus Magnus; groote means great.
biblical_def: Gerard Groote was a prosperous and worldly scholar of Deventer who, converted about 1374, gave his house to poor women and began to preach in the vernacular across the diocese of Utrecht, denouncing clerical concubinage and simony with such effect that the bishop was persuaded to silence him. Around him gathered men and women who lived in common houses without taking monastic vows, supporting themselves by copying manuscripts and teaching: the Brethren of the Common Life. The pattern was taken from Act 4:32, where the multitude of believers “were of one heart and of one soul” and held all things in common, and the quiet industry from 1Th 4:11, “that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands.” Their schools became the best in northern Europe, and Erasmus, Thomas à Kempis, and later Luther's own teachers passed through them. The movement produced vernacular Scripture, serious catechizing, and a piety of the heart rather than the shrine — and in that it was a seedbed of the Reformation a century and a half before it came.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a brotherhood as an association of men for any purpose; a fraternity; and common as belonging equally to more than one, or to many indefinitely.
webster_full: BROTH'ERHOOD, n. The state or quality of being a brother.
2. An association of men for any purpose, as a society of monks; a fraternity.
COM'MON, a. Belonging equally to more than one, or to many indefinitely.
scriptures: Act 4:32
And the multitude of them that believed were of one heart and of one soul: neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common.
Act 2:44
And all that believed were together, and had all things common;
And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works:
And that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you;
corruption_summary: Groote's houses show how much reform is possible without a doctrine of justification, and therefore how little.
corruption_paragraphs: The Devotio Moderna achieved almost everything a reform movement can achieve short of the gospel: honest clergy, educated laity, Scripture in the language of the people, communities of real charity, and a piety that had no use for relics or indulgences. And it left the doctrine of salvation untouched, so that its spirituality remained one of imitation and interior discipline rather than of justification by faith. That is why the Brethren could educate both Erasmus and the men who taught Luther, and why only one of those two could finish the work.

A second caution concerns the common life itself. Act 2:44 and Act 4:32 describe a voluntary and local sharing in the Jerusalem church under particular conditions, and the New Testament nowhere makes it a rule binding every congregation; 1Th 4:11 assumes private labour and private households. Groote wisely refused to impose vows, which kept his houses free of the monastic error, but communities built on the Jerusalem pattern have repeatedly hardened into something Scripture did not command. The recovery is Heb 10:24 — “let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works” — practised in the ordinary congregation, with the gospel at the centre.
roots_summary: Greek koinos (G2839), common; homothumadon (G3661), with one accord; paroxusmos (G3948), a provoking, a stirring up.
roots_lines: Greek koinos (G2839) — common, shared; Acts 2:44, Acts 4:32.
Greek psuche (G5590) — soul; Acts 4:32.
Greek paroxusmos (G3948) — a stirring up, a provoking; Hebrews 10:24.
Greek philotimeomai (G5389) — to study, to make it one's ambition; 1 Thessalonians 4:11.
Greek hesuchazo (G2270) — to be quiet, to rest; 1 Thessalonians 4:11.

“and had all things common” (Act 2:44) — voluntary, local, and not commanded of all.
“that ye study to be quiet, and to do your own business” (1Th 4:11) — the Brethren's industry.

pos: n. (Thomas à Kempis, c. 1380–1471, canon regular of Mount St Agnes, reputed author of The Imitation of Christ, the most widely read devotional book after the Bible)
etymology: Latin Thomas a Kempis, Thomas of Kempen, his birthplace in the Rhineland; his family name was Hemerken, little hammer.
biblical_def: Thomas à Kempis was schooled by the Brethren of the Common Life at Deventer, entered the house of canons at Zwolle, and lived there some seventy years, copying manuscripts and writing. The Imitation of Christ is the flower of the Devotio Moderna: four books of short chapters on self-knowledge, humility, the cross and the inner life, written in a Latin so plain that it has carried into every language. Its first principle is Mat 16:24, “If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me,” and its aim is 1Jn 2:6, that he who abides in Christ “ought himself also so to walk, even as he walked.” Php 2:5 is the whole programme — “Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus.” Protestants have read it from the beginning: Wesley and Newton loved it, and so have many Reformed pastors. Its limitation is structural. The Imitation is a book about following, and it says comparatively little about being justified, so a reader who takes it as a complete guide will be given a Christ to copy before he is given a Christ to trust.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines imitation as the act of following in manners, or copying in form; the act of making the similitude of any thing, or of attempting a likeness.
webster_full: IMITA'TION, n. The act of following in manners, or of copying in form.
2. That which is made or produced as a copy; likeness; resemblance.
3. In preaching, the application of a general doctrine to a particular case.
scriptures: Then said Jesus unto his disciples, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.
He that saith he abideth in him ought himself also so to walk, even as he walked.
Php 2:5
Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus:
For I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you.
corruption_summary: The Imitation gives a Christ to copy, and a reader who meets Him there first will try to follow before he has been forgiven.
corruption_paragraphs: The call to imitate is Scripture's own — Joh 13:15, “I have given you an example, that ye should do as I have done to you” — and no Reformed reader should flinch at it. The difficulty is order. Imitation is the fruit of union with Christ and follows justification; made the starting point, it becomes a law the reader cannot keep and a measure by which he will either despair or deceive himself. The Imitation assumes the medieval sacramental system for the forgiveness it rarely discusses, which is why it can be so searching about the heart and so quiet about the ground of acceptance.

Read in its place the book is a gift. Its chapters on self-knowledge and on the vanity of learning for its own sake are as sharp as anything in Puritan practical divinity, and its refusal of the shrine-piety of its age is bracing. The discipline for a Protestant reader is to come to it with Romans already in hand: first the imputed righteousness of Christ received by faith alone, then the mind of Christ formed in the justified by the Spirit. Mat 16:24 is addressed to disciples, and self-denial is the shape of a saved life rather than the price of one.
roots_summary: Greek aparneomai (G533), to deny utterly; peripateo (G4043), to walk; hupodeigma (G5262), an example, a pattern.
roots_lines: Greek aparneomai (G533) — to deny utterly, to disown; Matthew 16:24.
Greek akoloutheo (G190) — to follow, to accompany; Matthew 16:24.
Greek peripateo (G4043) — to walk, to conduct oneself; 1 John 2:6.
Greek phroneo (G5426) — to be minded, to think; Philippians 2:5.
Greek hupodeigma (G5262) — an example, a pattern; John 13:15.

“ought himself also so to walk, even as he walked” (1Jn 2:6) — its aim.
“I have given you an example” (Joh 13:15) — imitation commanded, in its place.

pos: n. (Wessel Gansfort, c. 1419–1489, Dutch theologian of Groningen, called Lux Mundi, who attacked indulgences and the treasury of merits two generations before Luther)
etymology: Dutch Wessel Gansfort, of Groningen; also written Goesevort and Gansevoort.
biblical_def: Wessel Gansfort was schooled by the Brethren of the Common Life at Zwolle, studied and taught at Cologne, Louvain, Paris and Heidelberg, and returned to end his life in Groningen. He is the most interesting of the forerunners because he worked out so much of the Reformation's criticism on his own. He denied that the pope holds a treasury of merits to dispense; argued that an indulgence remits only canonical penalty and can touch neither guilt nor the judgment of God; held that the church is the communion of the elect rather than the hierarchy; made Scripture the judge of councils and popes; and taught that faith unites the soul to Christ so that His righteousness becomes the ground of acceptance. Rom 1:17 is the hinge — “The just shall live by faith” — and Rom 5:1 the consequence: “Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.” He died unmolested, protected by friends and by the vagueness of his reputation. Luther, who published a volume of his letters in 1522, remarked that if he had read Wessel earlier his enemies would have said he learned everything from him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines justification, in theology, as remission of sin and absolution from guilt and punishment; or an act of free grace by which God pardons the sinner and accepts him as righteous, on account of the atonement of Christ.
webster_full: JUSTIFICA'TION, n. In theology, remission of sin and absolution from guilt and punishment; or an act of free grace by which God pardons the sinner and accepts him as righteous, on account of the atonement of Christ.
2. Vindication; defense; the showing of a sufficient reason.
FAITH, n. The assent of the mind to the truth of a proposition or statement for which there is not absolute proof.
scriptures: Rom 1:17
For therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith: as it is written, The just shall live by faith.
Hab 2:4
Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith.
Rom 5:1
Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ:
Gal 5:1
Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
corruption_summary: Wessel shows that the Reformation's doctrine was being recovered from Scripture in several places at once, and that the Roman system therefore cannot call it a German novelty.
corruption_paragraphs: A standard Roman argument treats justification by faith alone as Luther's invention, a sixteenth-century German innovation unknown to the church before. Wessel Gansfort is one answer among several. A respected Catholic doctor, writing in the 1470s with no Lutheran influence available to him, reached the insufficiency of indulgences, the authority of Scripture over the hierarchy, and the imputed righteousness of Christ received by faith — because he was reading Paul. The doctrine was not invented in 1517; it was recovered, and it was being recovered wherever Rom 1:17 was read carefully.

The caution is against the opposite overstatement, which makes Wessel a Protestant before his time. He remained within the Roman communion, kept much of its sacramental theology, and nowhere drew the ecclesiological conclusions the Reformers drew. The forerunners prepared the ground; they did not finish the work, and a movement that needs them to have been secret Protestants is leaning on the wrong support. Gal 5:1 is the liberty at stake — “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free” — and the Reformation's warrant is the text, not a line of precursors.
roots_summary: Greek dikaioo (G1344), to justify, to declare righteous; pistis (G4102), faith; eleutheria (G1657), liberty.
roots_lines: Greek dikaiosune (G1343) — righteousness; Romans 1:17.
Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to justify, to declare righteous; Romans 5:1.
Greek pistis (G4102) — faith, trust; Romans 1:17.
Hebrew emunah (H530) — faithfulness, faith; Habakkuk 2:4.
Greek eleutheria (G1657) — liberty, freedom; Galatians 5:1.
usage: “The just shall live by faith” (Rom 1:17) — the hinge he had already found.
“but the just shall live by his faith” (Hab 2:4) — the prophet Paul cites.
“being justified by faith, we have peace with God” (Rom 5:1) — the consequence he drew.

pos: n. (Johann Ruchrat von Wesel, c. 1400–1481, German theologian and preacher of Worms, who attacked indulgences and papal authority and recanted before the Inquisition in 1479)
etymology: From Wesel on the Rhine; his family name was Ruchrat or Rucherat. Not Wessel Gansfort, nor John Wesley.
biblical_def: John of Wesel taught at Erfurt, where he was rector, and preached at Worms, and he said in public what many thought in private: that indulgences are a fraud upon the people, that the pope may err and a council may err, that Scripture alone binds the conscience, and that the elect are saved by God's choice and not by ecclesiastical machinery. He was old and ill when the Inquisition took him at Mainz in 1479. He was examined, his writings were produced against him, and he recanted, abjuring his errors publicly and burning his own books; he was nonetheless confined in an Augustinian monastery, where he died within two years. Luther, who had studied where Wesel had taught, spoke of him with sympathy rather than contempt. The Scriptures hold both the warning and the comfort. “whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven” (Mat 10:33) is not to be softened; and yet Luk 22:32 is spoken to a man who did deny, “when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren,” and Psa 103:14 says “he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to recant as to retract; to recall; to contradict a former declaration; and abjuration as a renunciation upon oath.
webster_full: RECANT', v.t. To retract; to recall; to contradict a former declaration.
RECANT', v.i. To recall words; to revoke a declaration or proposition; to unsay.
ABJURA'TION, n. A renunciation upon oath; the act of abjuring.
scriptures: But whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven.
But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust.
corruption_summary: John of Wesel is the forerunner who broke, and a church that can only honour the ones who burned has not understood its own doctrine of grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Protestant martyrology has a natural bias: it remembers Hus, who refused, and passes quickly over Wesel, who recanted. But a theology of sovereign grace has no room for contempt here. “he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust” (Psa 103:14) is said of men under pressure, and the apostle who denied his Lord three times by a fire was restored and commissioned. Mat 10:33 stands and is terrible, and it is not the whole of what Scripture says to the man who failed; Peter is the proof. The honest account names the recantation as a fall, declines to pretend otherwise, and leaves the man where he belongs, with his Judge.

The second corruption is the modern inversion, which treats the recantation as the sensible course and the martyr as a fanatic — a reading that makes confession negotiable whenever the cost is high. That empties 2Co 12:9 of its meaning, for the promise “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness” is given precisely so that weak men may stand. The recovery is to pray for grace to confess, to refuse to despise those who did not, and to notice that Wesel's doctrines outlived his abjuration: thirty-eight years later a monk from his own university nailed up the same objections, and did not recant.
roots_summary: Greek arneomai (G533 cognate G720), to deny; epistrepho (G1994), to turn back, to be converted; astheneia (G769), weakness.
roots_lines: Greek arneomai (G720) — to deny, to disown; Matthew 10:33.
Greek epistrepho (G1994) — to turn about, to be converted; Luke 22:32.
Greek sterizo (G4741) — to strengthen, to establish; Luke 22:32.
Greek astheneia (G769) — weakness, infirmity; 2 Corinthians 12:9.
Hebrew yetser (H3336) — frame, form, that which is fashioned; Psalm 103:14.

“when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren” (Luk 22:32) — spoken to one who denied.
“he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust” (Psa 103:14) — the Judge who knows the man.

pos: n. (Nicholas of Cusa, 1401–1464, cardinal-bishop of Brixen, author of On Learned Ignorance, conciliarist turned papalist, mathematician and speculative theologian)
etymology: Latin Nicolaus Cusanus, of Kues on the Moselle; Greek Nikolaos, conqueror of the people.
biblical_def: Nicholas of Cusa began as the ablest theorist of the conciliar party, arguing in De Concordantia Catholica that authority rises from the consent of the governed and that a council stands above the pope; he then changed sides, served Eugene IV as a diplomat, and spent his later life as a papal cardinal. His philosophy is more durable than his politics. De Docta Ignorantia argues that God is beyond every proportion the mind can form, so that the highest knowledge is a learned ignorance which knows that it does not comprehend; in God, he says, opposites coincide. Job 11:7 asks his question — “Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection?” — and Isa 55:8 gives the ground: “my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways.” 1Co 13:12 grants that “now we see through a glass, darkly.” He wrote De Pace Fidei after the fall of Constantinople, imagining a concord of religions under one faith in varied rites, and a careful study of the Koran to refute it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines incomprehensible as that which cannot be comprehended or understood; beyond the reach of human intellect; and ignorance as want of knowledge.
webster_full: INCOMPREHEN'SIBLE, a. That cannot be comprehended or understood; beyond the reach of human intellect; inconceivable.
IG'NORANCE, n. Want of knowledge or instruction; unenlightened state of the mind.
God is incomprehensible, and his ways past finding out.
scriptures: Job 11:7
Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection?
Isa 55:8
For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD.
For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
Joh 17:3
And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.
corruption_summary: Learned ignorance is a true doctrine with a dangerous edge, and Cusa's own peace of faith shows where the edge cuts.
corruption_paragraphs: That God is incomprehensible is confessed by every Reformed standard, and Cusa states it beautifully. The danger is the slide from God is not comprehended to God is not known, and from there to the conclusion that competing accounts of Him are all approximations of the same ineffable reality. De Pace Fidei takes that step, proposing one religion in a variety of rites, with Islam and Christianity as different garments on a single faith. Joh 17:3 forbids it: “this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.” The knowledge is real, definite and particular, and it is not a rite.

The modern descendant is the pluralist theology that cites divine mystery as the reason no revelation can be final — the same move with the Christology removed. Scripture holds the two truths together without strain: God dwells in light no man can approach, and the Son has declared Him; we see through a glass darkly, and what we see is true. Isa 55:8 humbles the reasoner without silencing the revelation. Keep Cusa's humility about the divine essence and refuse his concord of faiths.
roots_summary: Hebrew chaqar (H2713), to search out; Greek ainigma (G135), an enigma, darkly; ginosko (G1097), to know.
roots_lines: Hebrew chaqar (H2713) — to search out, to explore; Job 11:7.
Hebrew tachlith (H8503) — perfection, an end; Job 11:7.
Greek esoptron (G2072) — a mirror, a glass; 1 Corinthians 13:12.
Greek ainigma (G135) — an obscure saying, darkly; 1 Corinthians 13:12.
Greek ginosko (G1097) — to know, to come to know; John 17:3.
usage: “Canst thou by searching find out God?” (Job 11:7) — his question, well asked.
“my thoughts are not your thoughts” (Isa 55:8) — the ground of learned ignorance.
“that they might know thee the only true God” (Joh 17:3) — the knowledge that is definite.

pos: n. (the Council of Basel, 1431–1449, the high-water mark of conciliarism, which deposed Eugene IV, elected the antipope Felix V, and dissolved in failure)
etymology: Latin concilium; Basel on the Rhine, where the council first sat before part of it removed to Ferrara.
biblical_def: The Council of Basel was summoned under the decree of Constance requiring regular general councils, and it began well: it negotiated a settlement with the Hussites of Bohemia granting the cup to the laity, and it passed decrees against simony, concubinage and the abuse of appeals. Then it collided with the pope. Eugene IV ordered it dissolved; it refused, reaffirmed that a council is superior to a pope, and when he transferred the assembly to Ferrara in 1437 the majority stayed at Basel, declared him deposed in 1439, and elected Amadeus of Savoy as Felix V. Christendom now had a council and a pope each denying the other, and a second pope besides. Support drained away, Felix abdicated in 1449, and the council expired. Conciliarism never recovered. Pro 11:14 is true — “in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” — and Basel is the proof that a multitude of counsellors is not by itself a safeguard, for 1Co 14:33 says “God is not the author of confusion, but of peace,” and Basel ended in confusion of its own making.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a council as an assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice; and confusion as disorder; irregular mixture; tumultuous disorder.
webster_full: COUN'CIL, n. An assembly of men summoned or convened for consultation, deliberation and advice.
CONFU'SION, n. In a general sense, a mixture of several things promiscuously; hence, disorder; irregular mixture.
2. Tumult; want of order in society.
scriptures: Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints.
Jas 3:16
For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work.
And Jesus knew their thoughts, and said unto them, Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand:
corruption_summary: Basel tried to cure the papacy with a parliament and proved that a council without the Word is only another body of men.
corruption_paragraphs: Conciliarism was a real attempt at a real disease. The papacy of the fifteenth century was a scandal, and the Constance decree was an effort to put it under law. But the remedy mistook the nature of authority: it moved the final word from one man to an assembly, where Scripture places it in neither. A council may err, and Basel erred spectacularly, electing an antipope and so reproducing the schism it existed to prevent. Mat 12:25 pronounced the outcome in advance — “every city or house divided against itself shall not stand.”

The Reformed answer is not conciliar and not papal. Synods and councils are useful and may be called, and the 1689 Confession allows their counsel while denying them dominion over the churches; their decrees bind only so far as they agree with Scripture, which alone is the rule. Jas 3:16 diagnoses what Basel became: “where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work.” The recovery is a church governed by elders under the Word, which can receive the help of a synod without ever making the synod its judge.

roots_lines: Hebrew yoets (H3289) — a counsellor; Proverbs 11:14.
Hebrew teshuah (H8668) — safety, deliverance; Proverbs 11:14.
Greek akatastasia (G181) — confusion, instability; 1 Corinthians 14:33, James 3:16.
Greek zelos (G2205) — zeal, envying; James 3:16.
Greek merizo (G3307) — to divide, to part; Matthew 12:25.
usage: “in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14) — true, and not a guarantee.
“God is not the author of confusion, but of peace” (1Co 14:33) — against what Basel became.
“every city or house divided against itself shall not stand” (Mat 12:25) — the council's own end.
